newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy industrialists see 97 deficit/GDP at 3.4 pct.
newsitem.headline: Italy industrialists see 97 deficit/GDP at 3.4 pct.

text.p: Italy's deficit will come in at around 3.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 if interest rates remain unchanged and the government does not introduce fresh budget measures, Italian industrialists group Confindustria said in a report.
Confindustria added that they expected the deficit/GDP ratio to fall to 3.0 percent in 1998 against a government target of 2.8 percent.

The government has pledged to reduce the closely watched ratio to three percent this year, from 6.7 percent in 1996, to meet one of the key criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for countries wishing to join the single European currency.

Confindustria said information about government spending made it difficult to say precisely where the deficit/GDP ratio would end up this year, adding that it could be anywhere between 3.2-3.6 percent, with 3.4 percent the mid-level.
"The forecast is based on the hypothesis that interest rates stay at the current high levels and (the forecast) would improve if conditions for a rate cut were created," the report said.

However, Confindustria said it expected the government to introduce additional budget measures towards the end of the year to push the deficit down. "On this basis, we would expect a final ratio of 3.2 percent (in 1997)," the report said.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has said he would resign if Italy failed to become a founder member of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
The government has said it does not expect to introduce fresh deficit cuts before the end of the year, saying it is already on course to hit the three percent target in 1997.

The official discount rate is at 6.75 percent, unchanged since January, despite steadily falling inflation and constant calls from industrialists, unions and the government for the Bank of Italy to ease its tight monetary policy.

To hit the deficit/GDP goal of 2.8 percent in 1998, the government has already said it will cut the deficit next year by some 25 trillion lire through a mix of spending cuts and raising fresh revenues.
However Confindustria said it did not expect all the planned deficit cutting measures to be effective. "It will be difficult to achieve spending cuts of 15 trillion lire," it said.
Nonetheless, it predicted that Italy still stood a good chance of joining the planned single European currency when founder members were picked at a European Union summit next May.

"This is especially possible when you consider that probably other major European countries will come forward in May 1998 with public finances for 1997 which are not too different from those of Italy and given the fact that in 1998 we will hit the three percent target," Confindustria said. -- Rome newsroom +396 6782501
